screens.title: Prepare and initialize config servers
screens.narratorSegment: Config servers hold the sharded cluster's metadata, so you must deploy them as a replica set for redundancy and durability. A typical production deployment uses three config server members so a majority is always available for writes. To initialize them, connect to one instance and run a replica set initiation that sets configsvr: true and names the replica set. For example, when you run the initiation, you will specify the replica set _id, mark configsvr true, and list members with host and port. A concrete example is initiating a configReplSet with hosts on ports 27019, 27020, and 27021. After initiation, verify each member reaches SECONDARY or PRIMARY state and that replication is healthy. A common misconception is treating config servers like ordinary shards; they are special: their dataset is the cluster metadata and should not host user data. Another mistake is deploying an even number of config servers, which can break majority-based decisions. The takeaway: always use an odd number of config server members, initialize them as a replica set with configsvr true, and verify replica set health before starting mongos routers. How will you confirm your config servers are healthy in your test environment?

keyIdea.title: Config server rule
keyIdea.text: Config servers must be a replica set (commonly three members) with configsvr: true; verify rs.status before proceeding.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Prepare config servers
Step-by-step
  1. Start three mongod instances with --configsvr and --replSet options on distinct hosts/ports.
  2. Connect to one config server with mongosh and run rs.initiate with configsvr:true and members listed.
  3. Run rs.status() to confirm PRIMARY/SECONDARY roles and replication health.
  4. Only after stable config servers, proceed to start mongos routers that reference the config replica set.
Common mistake: Using an even number of config servers or skipping rs.initiate; both prevent reliable metadata consensus.
Example initiation (connect to port 27019)
// Connect to one config server instance
// mongo --port 27019

rs.initiate(
  {
    _id: "configReplSet",
    configsvr: true,
    members: [
      { _id: 0, host: "cfg1.example.com:27019" },
      { _id: 1, host: "cfg2.example.com:27020" },
      { _id: 2, host: "cfg3.example.com:27021" }
    ]
  }
)
Key Takeaway

Initialize config servers as a replica set and confirm with rs.status before starting mongos instances.

screens.title: Start mongos routers
screens.narratorSegment: mongos instances act as query routers; applications connect to mongos rather than to shard members directly. Each mongos must be started with a --configdb parameter that names the config server replica set and lists at least one member address. In practice you run at least two mongos processes across different hosts for redundancy. A concrete command includes the replica set name followed by member host:port pairs. After starting mongos, check its logs to confirm it discovered the config replica set and can read metadata. A frequent misconception is that mongos stores metadata locally; it does not. mongos consults config servers dynamically and caches metadata for routing, but correct operation depends on the config server replica set being healthy. If mongos cannot contact the config servers, it cannot route writes or reads for sharded collections. The takeaway: start multiple mongos routers with correct --configdb settings and verify discovery in logs before adding shards. Start mongos routers means mongos reads config server metadata; launch multiple mongos instances with the correct --configdb string and confirm connectivity.. In practical terms, run mongos instances that point to the config server replica set. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Start mongos
Recommended steps
  • Start at least two mongos instances for redundancy and load distribution.
  • Provide the --configdb parameter with the config replica set name and member addresses.
  • Confirm mongos logs for successful config server discovery before accepting client traffic.
Misconception: mongos is not a metadata keeper; it routes using config server metadata and should be treated as a stateless query router.
Example mongos start commands
# Start mongos instance 1
mongos --configdb configReplSet/cfg1.example.com:27019,cfg2.example.com:27020,cfg3.example.com:27021 --port 27017 --bind_ip_all --logpath /var/log/mongodb/mongos1.log --fork

# Start mongos instance 2
mongos --configdb configReplSet/cfg1.example.com:27019,cfg2.example.com:27020,cfg3.example.com:27021 --port 27018 --bind_ip_all --logpath /var/log/mongodb/mongos2.log --fork
Key Takeaway

Run multiple mongos routers configured with the correct configdb string and verify they discover config servers.

screens.title: Add replica-set shards to the cluster
screens.narratorSegment: After config servers and mongos are running, the next step is to register each shard, which should be a replica set, with the cluster through sh. addShard. You provide the replica set name followed by a slash and at least one member host:port so mongos can reach that set. A concrete example registers two replica sets named shardReplSetA and shardReplSetB with their member addresses. Once added, verify the cluster topology using sh. status to see each shard listed. A common error is attempting to add a standalone mongod as a shard; in production every shard should be a replica set to ensure high availability. Another pitfall is using incorrect host addresses or unreachable members, which prevents the shard from registering. The balancer will not move data to a shard until it is properly registered. The takeaway: always add shards as replica sets via sh. addShard, check sh. status immediately, and ensure network reachability and replica-set health before relying on a new shard. Add replica-set shards to the cluster means use sh.addshard with the replica set name and at least one reachable member; verify presence with sh.status.. In practical terms, register each shard with sh.addshard and verify with sh.status. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Add shards
Why shards must be replica sets

Replica sets provide redundancy and automatic failover. Registering a shard that is not a replica set sacrifices availability and prevents proper chunk migration during failures.

Verification steps:
  • Run sh.addShard with the replica set string.
  • Run sh.status() and confirm the shard appears under the shards list.
  • Check replica set health on shard members with rs.status().
Example: register two shards
// Connect to mongos on port 27017
// mongosh --port 27017

sh.addShard("shardReplSetA/sra1.example.com:27001,sra2.example.com:27002")
sh.addShard("shardReplSetB/srb1.example.com:27003,srb2.example.com:27004")

// Verify
sh.status()
Key Takeaway

Register shards as replica sets with sh.addShard and confirm with sh.status and rs.status on shard members.

screens.title: Enable sharding for a database
screens.narratorSegment: Before sharding a collection, you must explicitly enable sharding for its database. This is a deliberate safety step that prevents unintentional sharding operations across databases. The command to enable database sharding tells the cluster metadata that collections within this database are permitted to be sharded. A common beginner error is trying to shard a collection and receiving an error that sharding is not enabled; the missing step is the database-level enabling command. For example, enabling sharding for a database named inventory is a single command executed through a mongos-connected shell. After enabling sharding, you can choose a shard key and run the shardCollection command. The verification step is simple: if sh. enableSharding was successful, the cluster's metadata reflects the database as sharding-enabled and sh. shardCollection will proceed. The takeaway: always enable sharding on the database before attempting to shard any collection, and include this as a checklist item in your deployment playbook. Enable sharding for a database means run the database-level enable command before trying to shard collections; forgetting this causes a common error when running shardcollection.. In practical terms, allow collections in a database to be sharded before sharding any collection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Enable database sharding
Why enable sharding per database?

This explicit action prevents accidental sharding of collections and allows administrators to plan shard keys and distribution before changes occur. The cluster records that the database is allowed to host sharded collections.

Misconception: Enabling the database immediately shards all collections. It does not; it simply allows collections to be sharded when you explicitly shard them.
Example command
// Connect to mongos
// mongosh --port 27017

sh.enableSharding("inventory")
Key Takeaway

Enable sharding at the database level before sharding collections in that database to avoid errors and accidental operations.

screens.title: Shard a collection with sh.shardCollection
screens.narratorSegment: The sh. shardCollection command tells MongoDB to split a collection into chunks and distribute those chunks across available shards based on the shard key you provide. You can choose a hashed shard key to spread documents evenly according to a hash of a field, which is useful for monotonically increasing keys like numeric IDs. Alternatively, a ranged key composed of multiple fields can support range queries by preserving ordering. For example, you might shard inventory. products on a hashed productId to spread inserts across shards, or shard mydatabase. orders on a compound {orderDate, userId} ranged key to support date-range queries. When you shard an existing collection, MongoDB creates chunks and migrates them; this can take time and is coordinated by the balancer. A common misconception is that hashed keys are always better; hashed keys scatter data and can harm range query performance. The takeaway: choose hashed keys for even distribution of point lookups and compound ranged keys when query patterns benefit from ordered ranges. After running shardCollection, monitor chunk migration and balancer activity until distribution stabilizes. Shard a collection with sh.shardCollection means use hashed keys for even write distribution; use ranged or compound keys when range queries or locality matter. monitor balancer after sharding.. In practical terms, use hashed and ranged shard keys to distribute data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Shard a collection
When to use hashed vs ranged keys
  • Hashed: evens out writes for sequential identifiers; loses range query efficiency.
  • Ranged/compound: preserves sort order for range queries; can create hotspots if key is monotonically increasing.
  • Compound keys combine fields to improve distribution for multi-dimensional access patterns.
Example shardCollection commands
// Shard users collection with a hashed userId
sh.shardCollection("mydatabase.users", { "userId": "hashed" })

// Shard orders collection with a compound ranged key
sh.shardCollection("mydatabase.orders", { "orderDate": 1, "userId": 1 })
Key Takeaway

Pick the shard key based on write distribution and query patterns; validate with a development workload before production.

screens.title: Balancer and chunk migration
screens.narratorSegment: The balancer is a background process that moves chunks between shards to maintain an even distribution of data. When you shard a collection, MongoDB splits the data into chunks based on the shard key and places them on shards. If one shard grows disproportionately, the balancer schedules migrations to redistribute chunks. You can observe balancer activity with sh. status and monitor chunk counts per shard. A concrete example: after sh. shardCollection on an existing collection, MongoDB will create chunks and the balancer moves them to balance chunk count. A common misconception is that the balancer instantly balances data; in reality, balancing is gradual and coordinated to limit network and input and output impact. Also, migrations require connectivity and healthy replica sets on shard members; if a shard's replica set is unhealthy, chunk migration may stall. The takeaway: rely on the balancer for long-term balance but plan initial chunking and monitor migration; test balancing behavior with representative datasets in staging. Balancer and chunk migration means balancer migrates chunks gradually to maintain even distribution; it requires healthy, reachable shard replica sets to operate.. In practical terms, how mongodb distributes chunks and evens out load over time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Balancer & chunks
How chunk migration works
  • Chunks are ranges of shard-key values that group documents for migration.
  • The balancer schedules chunk moves to equalize chunk counts across shards.
  • Migrations occur gradually to limit impact and require healthy replication on source and target shards.
Operational notes
Monitor with sh.status and collection distribution commands. If migrations stall, inspect network, replica set health, and mongos logs for errors. Avoid big sudden migrations in production without staging verification.
Common mistake

Expecting instant balance; balancing is progressive and depends on chunk boundaries and cluster health.

screens.title: Shard key selection pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Picking the wrong shard key is one of the most consequential mistakes when implementing sharding. Low-cardinality fields concentrate documents on few shards, producing hotspots and poor parallelism. Monotonically increasing keys, such as timestamps or auto-incrementing IDs, can concentrate writes on the most recent chunk and cause a single-shard write hotspot. Conversely, a hashed key can spread writes evenly but reduces range-query efficiency. A concrete example: sharding on a field with only a handful of possible values will likely pack data onto a few shards, while sharding on a hashed unique productId will distribute inserts fairly evenly. Mitigations include using compound keys that incorporate a high-cardinality field, applying hashed keys for write-heavy point-access workloads, or introducing application-level sharding prefixes. Also test your shard key selection using representative query patterns in a staging environment; changing a shard key on a large production collection is complex and disruptive. The takeaway: choose a shard key based on your read and write patterns, and validate distribution with representative data before production rollout. Shard key selection pitfalls means avoid low-cardinality or monotonically increasing keys; choose keys aligned with query patterns and test distribution.. In practical terms, common mistakes and how to mitigate hotspots and uneven distribution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Adding a new shard to a running cluster
screens.narratorSegment: To scale out, you can add a new replica-set shard to an existing sharded cluster. Use sh. addShard with the new replica set name and at least one member address. After the shard is registered, the balancer will begin moving chunks to incorporate the new capacity. Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Lab: shard products
Lab steps

screens.title: Common operational pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Operational pitfalls during sharded cluster setup frequently stem from replica set misconfiguration, network issues, and insufficient security. If a shard's replica set has too few members, lacks an arbiter where appropriate, or contains unhealthy secondaries, both availability and chunk migrations suffer. Network latency between mongos, config servers, and shards can significantly slow metadata operations and migrations. Security oversights, such as leaving authentication disabled, expose administrative interfaces and can permit unauthorized configuration changes. A concrete example of a common mistake is forgetting to enable authentication from the start; in that case, anyone with network access could add shards or change shard keys. Mitigation steps include: provision each shard as a proper replica set with multiple members, test network latency and routing between components, and enable authentication and authorization early in staging. The takeaway: operational readiness is as critical as correct commands—verify replica sets, network health, and security settings before accepting production traffic. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn the concrete steps to deploy a basic MongoDB sharded cluster and why each component matters for correctness and availability. We'll focus on initializing config server replica sets, starting mongos query routers, registering replica-set shards, enabling database sharding, and issuing shardCollection with appropriate keys. You will see command examples and learn how to verify sharding status. This matters because a misconfigured cluster can create hotspots, uneven storage, or even reduce availability when a replica set is incomplete. For example, three config server replicas provide metadata redundancy; without a healthy config server replica set, the cluster cannot track chunk placement reliably. We also cover common pitfalls such as choosing low-cardinality keys or forgetting to enable sharding on a database before sharding a collection. By the end of this module you will be able to run the core mongosh commands to register shards, enable sharding, and shard collections safely in a controlled environment. Consider how you would test a shard strategy with realistic query patterns before you change a production shard key.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to perform core sharding operations and reason about their effects. First, you will outline the end-to-end process to build a basic sharded cluster, from initializing config server replica sets to starting mongos routers and registering shard replica sets. Second, you will execute mongosh commands to enable sharding for a database and to shard a collection; you'll understand the commands' intent and how to verify outcomes. Third, you'll add new replica-set shards to an existing cluster and confirm they are available to the balancer. Finally, you'll identify common pitfalls in shard key selection and configuration, and apply strategies to avoid hotspots and uneven distribution. Each objective includes a brief mnemonic or verification step to help you remember the command or concept and a small competency milestone to check your progress.

These objectives emphasize the practical skills you need to operate a sharded cluster safely. You'll practice initiating config server replica sets and confirming their replica set status, because the cluster metadata relies on healthy config servers. You'll also run mongos instances with a correct --configdb parameter so routers can discover metadata. You will add replica-set shards and confirm chunk distribution via sh. status and collection-level distribution commands. Finally, you'll practice a hands-on lab to shard a products collection with a hashed product identifier and then verify the balancer activity and chunk migration. Each skill includes a small verification step: inspect replica set health, check mongos logs for config discovery, and run sh. status to confirm shards and chunk counts. These concrete checks prevent common deployment mistakes and help you catch problems early during staging before production rollout.

Config servers hold the sharded cluster's metadata, so you must deploy them as a replica set for redundancy and durability. A typical production deployment uses three config server members so a majority is always available for writes. To initialize them, connect to one instance and run a replica set initiation that sets configsvr: true and names the replica set. For example, when you run the initiation, you will specify the replica set _id, mark configsvr true, and list members with host and port. A concrete example is initiating a configReplSet with hosts on ports 27019, 27020, and 27021. After initiation, verify each member reaches SECONDARY or PRIMARY state and that replication is healthy. A common misconception is treating config servers like ordinary shards; they are special: their dataset is the cluster metadata and should not host user data. Another mistake is deploying an even number of config servers, which can break majority-based decisions. The takeaway: always use an odd number of config server members, initialize them as a replica set with configsvr true, and verify replica set health before starting mongos routers. How will you confirm your config servers are healthy in your test environment?

mongos instances act as query routers; applications connect to mongos rather than to shard members directly. Each mongos must be started with a --configdb parameter that names the config server replica set and lists at least one member address. In practice you run at least two mongos processes across different hosts for redundancy. A concrete command includes the replica set name followed by member host:port pairs. After starting mongos, check its logs to confirm it discovered the config replica set and can read metadata. A frequent misconception is that mongos stores metadata locally; it does not. mongos consults config servers dynamically and caches metadata for routing, but correct operation depends on the config server replica set being healthy. If mongos cannot contact the config servers, it cannot route writes or reads for sharded collections. The takeaway: start multiple mongos routers with correct --configdb settings and verify discovery in logs before adding shards. Start mongos routers means mongos reads config server metadata; launch multiple mongos instances with the correct --configdb string and confirm connectivity.. In practical terms, run mongos instances that point to the config server replica set. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

After config servers and mongos are running, the next step is to register each shard, which should be a replica set, with the cluster through sh. addShard. You provide the replica set name followed by a slash and at least one member host:port so mongos can reach that set. A concrete example registers two replica sets named shardReplSetA and shardReplSetB with their member addresses. Once added, verify the cluster topology using sh. status to see each shard listed. A common error is attempting to add a standalone mongod as a shard; in production every shard should be a replica set to ensure high availability. Another pitfall is using incorrect host addresses or unreachable members, which prevents the shard from registering. The balancer will not move data to a shard until it is properly registered. The takeaway: always add shards as replica sets via sh. addShard, check sh. status immediately, and ensure network reachability and replica-set health before relying on a new shard. Add replica-set shards to the cluster means use sh.addshard with the replica set name and at least one reachable member; verify presence with sh.status.. In practical terms, register each shard with sh.addshard and verify with sh.status. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Before sharding a collection, you must explicitly enable sharding for its database. This is a deliberate safety step that prevents unintentional sharding operations across databases. The command to enable database sharding tells the cluster metadata that collections within this database are permitted to be sharded. The sh. shardCollection command tells MongoDB to split a collection into chunks and distribute those chunks across available shards based on the shard key you provide. You can choose a hashed shard key to spread documents evenly according to a hash of a field, which is useful for monotonically increasing keys like numeric IDs. Alternatively, a ranged key composed of multiple fields can support range queries by preserving ordering. For example, you might shard inventory. products on a hashed productId to spread inserts across shards, or shard mydatabase. orders on a compound {orderDate, userId} ranged key to support date-range queries. When you shard an existing collection, MongoDB creates chunks and migrates them; this can take time and is coordinated by the balancer. A common misconception is that hashed keys are always better; hashed keys scatter data and can harm range query performance. The takeaway: choose hashed keys for even distribution of point lookups and compound ranged keys when query patterns benefit from ordered ranges. The balancer is a background process that moves chunks between shards to maintain an even distribution of data. When you shard a collection, MongoDB splits the data into chunks based on the shard key and places them on shards. A concrete example: after sh. shardCollection on an existing collection, MongoDB will create chunks and the balancer moves them to balance chunk count. Picking the wrong shard key is one of the most consequential mistakes when implementing sharding. Low-cardinality fields concentrate documents on few shards, producing hotspots and poor parallelism. Monotonically increasing keys, such as timestamps or auto-incrementing IDs, can concentrate writes on the most recent chunk and cause a single-shard write hotspot. Conversely, a hashed key can spread writes evenly but reduces range-query efficiency. A concrete example: sharding on a field with only a handful of possible values will likely pack data onto a few shards, while sharding on a hashed unique productId will distribute inserts fairly evenly. Mitigations include using compound keys that incorporate a high-cardinality field, applying hashed keys for write-heavy point-access workloads, or introducing application-level sharding prefixes. Also test your shard key selection using representative query patterns in a staging environment; changing a shard key on a large production collection is complex and disruptive. The takeaway: choose a shard key based on your read and write patterns, and validate distribution with representative data before production rollout. Operational pitfalls during sharded cluster setup frequently stem from replica set misconfiguration, network issues, and insufficient security. If a shard's replica set has too few members, lacks an arbiter where appropriate, or contains unhealthy secondaries, both availability and chunk migrations suffer. Security oversights, such as leaving authentication disabled, expose administrative interfaces and can permit unauthorized configuration changes. A concrete example of a common mistake is forgetting to enable authentication from the start; in that case, anyone with network access could add shards or change shard keys.
